source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Continue conventional sharps when annual staff training is documented, because engineering controls are optional if workers understand needlestick risks.","B":"Allow each worker to decide whether to use a safety device, because employer selection of engineering controls is not required for bloodborne-pathogen compliance.","C":"Evaluate and implement an effective, clinically appropriate safer medical device, such as a needleless system or sharp with engineered injury protection in use.","D":"Replace disposable sharps with reusable needles whenever possible, because repeated sterilization is the preferred engineering control for needlestick prevention."}}
source_row.rationale: OSHA requires employers to use engineering and work-practice controls to minimize bloodborne-pathogen exposure and to evaluate and implement effective, clinically appropriate safety-engineered sharps when available. Option C states that requirement. Option A incorrectly treats training as a substitute for engineering controls. Option B incorrectly shifts the employer's control-selection obligation entirely to individual workers. Option D substitutes reusable needles for the safer-device controls OSHA describes.
source_row.source_detail: OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens — Evaluating and Controlling Exposure: engineering and work-practice controls must minimize exposure; employers must evaluate and implement effective, clinically appropriate safer medical devices such as needleless systems and sharps with engineered sharps-injury protection when available. Current OSHA bloodborne-pathogens requirements and guidance; rechecked 2026-08-15. source_row.stem: A hospital is reviewing sharps safety after a needlestick injury. Which OSHA requirement is most relevant when an effective, clinically appropriate safer device is available?
